items.question: How do you decide what level of understanding of the brain is useful as inspiration for your AI research?
items.object: The brain and evolution as sources of inspiration for AI research
items.answer:
For me, I really like to get inspired from the brain and generally evolution. The main reason is that I think it has a lot of data to train itself in a natural way of training. One thing that we can see now is a very evolved version of a very complicated biological brain, and so it's a great source of inspiration. But when I'm saying that, I don't mean that I want to replicate the brain and fully do something that the brain does, because most of the time we don't know what that is, actually.

I think there are different levels of understanding about how the brain works. The first one is, we know it works. That's the first level. The second level of understanding is that there are some modules in the brain, each of them responsible for different parts, and we have memory and other things, and that's generally the process. I think the hard part when we want to get inspired from the brain is at what level of granularity we want to focus on the brain and get inspired from that. Because if you go too much into the details, like how the brain works, there are two issues. One is you're overfitting ourselves to one specific form of intelligence. Another one is that we don't actually know how the brain does that specific thing.

In all of the work that I have done, for example on Titans and Nested Learning, one thing that is happening is we can see that the models are facing some challenges in real-world applications. Then the question is: is that specific challenge solved by humans, and can a human do something to address that challenge and overcome it or not? Then the second question is how they can do that. In Titan, we discussed the surprise metric, and how the memory should be decomposed into short-term and long-term memory. But the point is there's a high chance that the brain is not exactly performing gradient descent to understand the surprise or something like that. That's just a high-level understanding of how the brain works. I think if we keep that as a source of inspiration, that level would be a great source. But if we go into more details, then potentially we might face some challenges, specifically because our understanding of the brain is changing over time, and so we might overfit to one specific design choice.

items.question: How do you understand the limitations of the current LLM paradigm that motivate your work on Nested Learning?
items.object: Limitations of the current LLM paradigm that motivate Nested Learning
items.answer:
About Nested Learning, I think one coin that's missing in the current models is about two parts. One is how they can adapt to the environment and the context that they are in. Another point is how the model can understand new knowledge and incorporate it into their parameters over time, so they can make sure that they don't face catastrophic forgetting, which means that one specific task that they have trained on is forgotten, and they don't have any skills in that specific direction. These two are important things about the current models, and they are facing a lot of challenges with that. If you have a very large model, then your model needs to be updated over time. That's generally the main reason you can see there is a knowledge cutoff for all of the LLMs that we know of. If you ask ChatGPT about specific information and say you are not allowed to use any tools for answering this question, then you might see there's a knowledge cutoff, and that's a little bit challenging to overcome.

If you just want to keep updating the models, there are two huge challenges. One is catastrophic forgetting, and another one is efficiency, because if I have a lot of parameters, you cannot keep updating all of the parameters. There are some solutions for that, and I think they are great, but I have some intuitions about why they might not perfectly work for continual learning. For example, one might say that they want to do supervised fine-tuning, SFT, or do some RL stuff. But the model can still face catastrophic forgetting. From the other side, at some point, you need to transfer all the knowledge that you have in your context and pass it to the actual parameters of the model. If you just keep summarizing the tokens, if you just keep the tokens and want to do everything about the memory and learning process in the token space, then the main issue would be at some point you really pass the context lengths of the LLMs. Potentially, you will face some challenges in that direction.

Considering all these things, the main issue with the current LLM paradigm is that they cannot continually learn and obtain new knowledge and new skills over time. Also, they are limited in understanding different levels of abstraction of the world. Everything that is done in science is to do something that can explain the world in the simplest way possible. That's generally the way we can learn something, because we don't want to keep everything. We want to understand underlying patterns that can describe that specific data, that specific knowledge, and so on and so forth. This compression process and how we can understand different levels of abstraction from the data that we have is something that the current LLMs fall short on somehow.

items.question: How do you think an ideal continually learning AI should operate?
items.object: The technical design of an ideal continually learning AI
items.answer:
From the technical point of view, I think generally the entire research, most of the research in the past 40 years, is built on a paradigm that says we have a pre-training or generally a training phase, and we have a test phase. But the point is, if we have continual learning, we can see there are a lot of recent studies about continual learning, how we can do that, and how we can overcome a lot of challenges. A true continual learner doesn't have a test and train time. Potentially, if we hear this name in any design choice, it means it's not a true continual learner, because there is no test, there is no train time. The question is, is it a uniform process for the model or not?

My personal opinion is that we still need at least two phases. We should have one phase that the model is active. It actively receives information, whether through the user query, or for example vision models, word models, or anything similar. The model receives some information and generally performs some computation on the input data, and it's active at that point. On the other hand, there is another phase where the model does not have to wait for the input data. It might not receive any input data. It's completely locked from the world outside of it. But the question is, even at that time, should the model be static without performing computation or doing something, or does the model need to start thinking about some process, thinking about the data that it has inside its parameters, and so on? We can break the process into two parts: one is the active phase, and another one is potentially sleep time, because there is no input but still the artificial brain, or the model itself, is trying to perform some computation.

I think that's a good way of defining different phases in this direction of continual learning. A good model performs very well on both sides. It should receive the information properly, encode it, process it, and understand it in the best way possible. On the other hand, when it goes to sleep time, it should start processing what it has learned before and use that for self-improvement. That's what I think an ideal model should do from the technical point of view.

items.question: How do you see Nested Learning addressing the computational cost of keeping large models updated over time?
items.object: Nested Learning as a way to make continual model updates efficient
items.answer: I think there are a lot of challenges. The models that we know right now are really large. Even a simple academic paper presenting a new LLM or architecture needs to perform some experiments on models with billions of parameters, 1 billion, 2 billion, or something like that. Generally, that's a very large model that requires a lot of computation if you want to keep that model updated over time, and it needs some techniques to somehow make this process possible. For us, when we were thinking about this direction, it was a time that some ideas about Nested Learning started. If you think about Nested Learning, at each timestamp we don't have to update everything. We just need to update a small subset of all parameters. Potentially, that is a way to overcome the challenges about efficiency.

items.object: The two phases of an ideal continually learning model
items.answer: I think an ideal model should have two phases. One, generally, it should be a continual learner. It should interact with the world. Also, it should have two phases: one is a very active process, and another one is about self-improvement and how it can consolidate its memory, understand the knowledge, connect different things that seem to be irrelevant, and so on, and everything similar that our brain also does when we go to sleep.

items.question: Why do you think AI development should focus on what humans want from AI?
items.object: Human needs as a goal for AI development
items.answer: That's just my personal opinion and might be completely wrong, but I think we shouldn't focus too much on what humans can do. Instead, we need to focus more on what humans want from AI. I think if we think about it, we don't want to create something that is very similar to us. That's also a very interesting direction, but I'm personally not really interested in that. I think we have a great design for humans, but on the AI side, we need AI models that are capable of understanding what we want. For example, I think the current paradigm of LLMs, you can see that they're great after some time when we have more features. For example, ChatGPT has the memory now, and Claude has some features, Gemini and everything. Now they are more capable of understanding what you want. When you say, for example, write this image for me, they can simply write that for you. I think that's a very promising direction in general, because we don't want to replicate humans. I think we want to have a new form of intelligence that is proper and designed in a good way that understands human needs, so it can help people do a lot of things that they might face some challenges with without LLMs.

items.question: How do you understand inspiration from the human brain in your work on “LLMs Need Sleep”?
items.object: Brain-inspired AI and the meaning of “LLMs Need Sleep”
items.answer: Here again, we can get inspired from the human, but we need to understand why we want to get inspired. Do we want to get inspired because we want to replicate what humans can do, or do we want to get inspired from nature to understand some underlying rules in nature? One extreme example is we cannot travel through time. If I come up with an idea that my AI model is trying to break the causality in the world, then potentially that might be a wrong idea or wrong direction because it is breaking some nature rules about our world. Let me give you another example. When we are talking about the title that we use, "LLMs Need Sleep," it doesn't mean that LLMs need to literally go to sleep and rest. It means that from the human brain, it seems there is a very general rule that it has two phases of learning and then another phase of processing it, consolidating the memory, and finding underlying patterns between the received data. That's a very high level of inspiration from the brain.

items.question: Why do you see multiple update frequencies and knowledge transfer as complementary parts of Nested Learning?
items.object: Update frequencies and knowledge transfer in Nested Learning
items.answer: We were working on Nested Learning for a very, very long time, potentially even more than one year and a half. The main issue that I personally had, and we discussed a lot in the group after the authors of the work, was it was really hard to formalize what we wanted to deliver. Even in the mathematical formulation, it was really hard to write it in a formal way and say what we want to exactly do in this paradigm. After some back-and-forth discussions, I think we came up with this specific framework, saying that there is a frequency of updates to somehow give time to each module to do something when it's waiting. I think that's the best way of describing why we need to have multiple frequencies. On the other hand, we need a knowledge transfer method to somehow transfer the knowledge from one level to another level. When the slow network is waiting for all the computation and information processing of the fast network, there should be some advantage for the slow network that we're paying all this cost for doing some computation by the fast network. That advantage comes when we have a good way of knowledge transfer between the fast network and the slow one, which is like lower level to the higher. The idea is that when we have a network updating really fast, then I can use that fast computation to give something to a slow computation side. A slower network or level can somehow focus on the higher-level knowledge abstraction of the data, and the more frequently updated network can focus on fast adaptation and how they can process the high-resolution data. Generally, that was the way that we could describe this framework, saying these two sides need to be there to complement each other. One is the frequency of update, and another one is the knowledge transfer between the levels.

items.question: How do you think increasing computation per parameter could make language models smarter?
items.object: Computation per parameter in language models
items.answer:
In my opinion, the current models are very efficient from one specific point of view. Why are they efficient? Because you can see that from what we can get from LLMs, they are very cheap. If you want to match their power in some tasks with humans, then potentially the cost would be very different. From that perspective, we can say that computation and the current LLM paradigms are very efficient, and we can perform more computation per parameter or artificial neuron that we have in our model. It can help us to have a smarter model. It's a very subjective term to describe this, but when we have more computation, it seems that we are performing some internal thinking.

A simple LLM structure based on transformers: when the token comes, I do some computation on the token, pass it through all the layers, and then predict the next token. That's how it works. But now let's assume that for this specific token, instead of just a simple pass of computation, I also perform more internal computation with respect to the past data, or combine or mix the data. In that case, I can see that the quality of next-token prediction for this specific design choice can potentially go up. Why is that? Because it can be interpreted as a form of internal thinking process. For each specific parameter that I have in my model, it is performing several computations. So, it's not just one parameter, one step of computation. It's one parameter, a couple of steps of computation. That's one advantage.

items.question: Why do you find it useful to describe backpropagation, pre-training, attention, and recurrent models as forms of in-context learning?
items.object: In-context learning as a unified account of model learning
items.answer: When we have a model that is adapting to the context very fast, then potentially that model can learn context. That's somehow one of the main messages that we try to deliver in Nested Learning, which was everything that we know of somehow is a form of in-context learning. I think it's a great thing in human language that we create new words, but on the other hand, if we just create a lot of words for the same concept, it can make us confused or misleading somehow. We should create new words to differentiate different concepts, but if we have one specific concept, we need to stick to one specific word that we have for that concept to avoid misleading processes or anything like that. From that perspective, we realize that we can say everything is just a form of in-context learning. We already know what in-context learning is. Now, we just need to understand how what we have already been doing is a form of in-context learning. That was the part where we started showing that backpropagation is a form of in-context learning, a form of associative memory. When it's a form of associative memory, then we can say the general pre-training phase of the model is a form of in-context learning. When we go to the context of attention or RNN, so on and so forth, again, it's a form of in-context learning. When we perform gradients, which we can define for any RNN based on gradient descent or other forms of optimization, we are doing some learning on the context that is happening right now. I think these two are the main things that Nested Learning is trying to address. One is generally more computation per neuron, and another one is adaptability and continual learning.

items.question: Why do you think a continuum memory system with MLP blocks that update at different frequencies is useful?
items.object: The continuum memory system in Hope Attention
items.answer:
We start from the transformer structure. In a transformer we have an attention block and then an MLP block. When the model is pre-trained, the MLP block is fixed. It's not changing anymore. It has all the information compressed during the pre-training. At inference time, attention is responsible for the context that it is getting, and the MLP block is responsible for the long-term memory and the very general knowledge of the world.

Now, let's simply extend this idea. A simple extension is that we can keep attention, and then instead of just one MLP block we have multiple MLP blocks. Each of them are updated with different frequency. When you have attention, you have fast adaptation to the context. Attention is very powerful. It's like a perfect memory. It caches everything, and so it's great. On the other hand, you might want to have multiple levels of memory. That's the part we define as continuum memory system. Instead of one block of MLP, we have multiple blocks of MLP. Your first MLP block is updated very fast. The first updating process of this MLP block can cause catastrophic forgetting, because this MLP block can forget information that it got a couple thousand tokens ago. But since the other MLP blocks have not updated so far, the knowledge that is forgotten by the first MLP block is still in their parameters. When we perform backpropagation through all these layers, the knowledge can come back. It provides a loop process in time. The first MLP block can forget something, but if that specific data sample or skill that is forgotten is important, then this can come back through the other MLP blocks, which have not been updated so far and still have the knowledge about that specific skill or data sample. That's a very simple way of extending the whole transformer block. We call this variant Hope Attention. It's a combination of attention plus multiple MLP blocks, and that's what we called Hope Attention.

items.question: Why do you expect self-modifying Titan to handle sequential reasoning better than attention in the Hope architecture?
items.object: Self-modifying Titan as a replacement for attention in the Hope architecture
items.answer:
Attention, as I mentioned, is a perfect memory. It can cache everything, it can scale, and it's fast. But the point is, the update of attention has infinite frequency. It means that attention doesn't know anything about the temporal dependency of all the tokens. It needs something like positional encoding, or even with the help of positional encoding, attention is not a great model for tasks that are sequential, tasks that require sequential reasoning or something like that. Our idea was to replace attention with another associative memory that maps keys to values. That's what attention does. We want to replace it with another module that tries to map keys to values, and one potential architecture here is Titan. We can simply replace it with Titan and have Titan plus continuum system.

But the point is, in initial sections of the paper, we discussed that if you have a simple linear process of updates, which is what is happening inside each chunk of Titan update, this process can somehow be weaker than the case when we have a self-referential process. Gradient descent or generally backpropagation is a form of self-referential process. The idea is that we want to learn how to learn and how to learn and how to learn. There are a lot of levels of how to learn, and computationally it's infeasible to implement all those levels. There is one idea by Schwitalla et al., the idea of a self-referential model. One of the ways that we can make a model self-referential when we have a key-value memory is the case that the model generates its own value.

Let's say that in our memory we want to memorize something. There is a specific event happening and you want to memorize it, or you want to memorize a specific word. In our brain, we have associative memory and are trying to map this specific word to another concept that we already knew, so we can memorize it. You definitely have seen some cases that, for example, you say, "I generate this specific word" or "I want to map this specific word to another word that I already knew," so I can remember that. We generate the value that we want to map our keys to, so we can memorize the key as well.

For the self-referential process, it's a very general concept, but in this specific design choice that we have in the paper, the value of the associative memory is generated by its own parameters. The model itself generates its own value and then tries to map keys to values. Potentially, this process is fully sequential. You cannot parallelize it in a simple format, and so it has a full understanding of the causality in our data. Potentially in tasks that require sequential thinking, sequential reasoning, or anything like that, we can expect that this model should work better than simple attention, because simple attention doesn't have the ability to sequentially understand the causality of the data at all. In the Hope architecture, we replace Titan with self-modifying Titan, which is exactly a Titan module where it generates its own value function, the value of the associative memory. That's Hope architecture: self-modifying Titan plus continuous memory system.

items.question: How do you distinguish a self-referential associative memory such as self-modifying Titan from a model with learned Q, K, and V projections?
items.object: Self-referential associative memory and self-modifying Titan
items.answer:
Generally in transformer, more accurately softmax attention, what is happening there is that we have a projection of Q, K, V, and then the output goes to attention. Attention doesn't have any control on the Q, K, V projections. When I'm saying that the model, or generally the associative memory, tries to generate its own value and then map keys to the value, I mean something like gradient descent. If we recall gradient descent, we can see that we have the previous state of W, which is W t minus the gradient of the loss function that we have. This is equal to the next state of the weights that we have. If you look at this process, you can break the gradients using the chain rule and write it into the gradients with respect to the outputs times the input data. Now, you can see that this is getting a form of associative memory, very similar to linear attention, because it's Wt plus 1 equals the previous state of W minus K, and K here is Xt, and then V, which is the gradient with respect to the outputs.

If you look at this process, it's very similar to linear attention or any linear recurrence model. The very interesting part is it is different from linear attention because if you look at the value, which is the gradient with respect to the outputs, this gradient with respect to the output is a function of Wt, a function of the current state of the weights. Basically, the value component of the keys and values that we have in associative memory is not from another component before this recurrence formula, but it is generated by this recurrent process every time. That's what is going on with this self-referential process.

In memory, let's say that in a very simple version of self-modifying Titan, if we want to design this as a simple Titan, what is happening is I have this X and then QKV projection; I project it into QKV and pass all of them to the Titan module. That's a simple Titan module. But if I want to have a self-modifying Titan, then all of these parameters of the projection of Q, K, and V are optimized inside the Titan module. Basically, the model has control of somehow modifying its own updating rule and somehow generating its own value for further memory. That's the main difference of these two.

items.question: What do you see as the main difference between inference in Hope models and the familiar transformer paradigm?
items.object: Inference in Hope Attention and the Hope architecture
items.answer:

For Hope Attention, I think it's very similar to the current paradigm, and the architecture is very similar to transformers. It's actual transformer architecture. We just replace the MLP block with multiple MLP blocks. When we want to do inference, the main difference comes from the fact that for each of the MLP blocks, we need to track where we are. Is it the time that we want to update the MLP block, or does it still have time to get updated? If it's the latter case, then we use the last updated state of that specific MLP for doing the inference. If it's time to get updated, then we first update it through all the backpropagation stuff and all of the tokens that we have seen so far in the current chunk. Then, when the weight is updated, we perform inference.

items.question: Why do you consider learning unfamiliar languages in context a revealing evaluation of a model's continual-learning capabilities?
items.object: Learning unfamiliar languages in context as an evaluation of continual learning
items.answer:
We have one continual-learning-style task that I personally really like. The idea is that we have a pretrained model, and there is one specific language that the model has not seen before. We want the model to learn that specific language in context. We have all the grammar, all the words, a dictionary of words, and we pass all of them through the model in context. Then the model learns the language, and then we ask, can you translate this specific text to English from that language to English? We can see that the model, not perfectly, but in very, very good quality, can translate that specific text. It seems that the model is capable of understanding that language in context and then using that for some translation task.

Let's go one step beyond that. Instead of one language, let's put two languages in context and ask the model to translate different text from each of these languages to English. In that case, we can see that the model almost collapses and cannot translate any of those languages. The model cannot handle its context well and fully understand each of the languages separately. That's generally a very hard challenge for transformer-based architectures. But when we change that architecture to Hope or Hope Attention, again we have attention, but we have multiple levels of in-context learning, multiple levels of MLP blocks. One thing that we can see is that when we increase the number of levels, the performance of the model in both of these languages gets better and better. Why is it happening? Because the model has a better way of memory management. It understands that temporal knowledge that is not very needed can be stored in the first MLP block, and more understanding of the language can pass to the more stable MLP blocks, later MLP blocks that are more stable. When we have more and more blocks, we can see the performance gets better and better. In my opinion, that's a very good evaluation for understanding that the model can learn in context and generally for continual learning.

items.question: How do you understand the relationship between a model's architecture and its optimization process in Nested Learning?
items.object: The relationship between architecture and optimization in Nested Learning
items.answer:

This is interconnected because the gradients of the optimization side are generated by the architecture. If you have a simple architecture, then the gradients are very simple. If you have a complicated architecture, the patterns in the gradients can be very complicated. When you have a momentum term, momentum is a form of associative memory that is trying to compress gradients. If your gradients are very complicated, you need a more powerful memory-management system for your momentum. If it's a very simple architecture, then even simple gradient descent without any momentum might work very well.

One of the arguments that we have in the paper is that we should see everything as an interconnected system and try to design something that all together results in a good model architecture, or generally a machine-learning model in a very general term. Another thing is that we wanted to deliver the message that the architecture side is very similar, or somehow exactly the same, as the optimization side. All of them are just some learning rule, and there is some learning process happening. The only difference between the architecture side and the optimization side is just a context. The context of the optimization algorithm is gradients; actually, the context is the set of gradients that we have. The context of the architecture side is a set of tokens that we have. Generally, they're very similar.

items.question: What role do you see dreaming playing in a continual-learning model's sleep process?
items.object: Dreaming as a process in continual-learning models
items.answer:

The memory-consolidation part can also be seen as a form of self-improvement, but if we have a specific task at hand and want to specifically optimize the model for one task, this is the place that we can do it. We can self-modify the model and fine-tune it, or generally use RL to update and self-modify it, so it can be more powerful in one specific task. That's one advantage of dreaming.

Another advantage is that in the dreaming process, we need to understand the connection of concepts that seem to be irrelevant, but are actually relevant. That's also what is happening in the dreaming process of humans. We can see very weird dreams because the brain is trying to understand the connection of very irrelevant concepts and see whether there is an underlying pattern in that. In the dreaming process, we need that as well, and to understand different aspects of how we need to combine different knowledge stored in different components of the model. That's another goal of dreaming. We can combine these into the sleep process, and after one step of sleep, the model has consolidated its own memory and also has a self-improving process on top of that.

We add some parameters and then we free them for the next step of consolidation. When we are in the first block, we add some components. Generally, it's a periodic process. We add components and remove them.

items.question: How do you understand the process of dreaming in a language model?
items.object: Dreaming and memory consolidation in language models
items.answer:
The concept of dreaming doesn't mean that it's exactly the same thing as dreaming in humans. It's just that at a very high level they seem to be very similar. Another point is that the concept of sleep and dreaming for a language model might be very different from dreaming and sleep for, for example, a vision model. Potentially a vision model might generate some images during dreaming. In this case of language modeling, we are generating text. But the framework is very general. It can adapt to any data modality.

When we are doing that for language modeling, what is happening is we generate some context, we generate some text. How do we generate that text? It's on-policy distillation, the same way that we discussed earlier. We have a model, we copy that, want to distill the knowledge from one level to the other, and we free the parameters of the slower level, and so on. We ask the smaller model, which has the knowledge of the context in its parameters, to generate some text. Then we want to train, or update is a better term to use, the actual model parameters on this dataset that is generated by the model. How do we train it? We start with one part of the sequence, just sample some of the tokens, and then ask the model to predict the next tokens in that sequence. That's similar to generating some synthetic data. If the model can perfectly predict the future tokens, it means that it already knew the knowledge that is stored in the previous block. But if it cannot properly predict the continuation of the sequence, it means that it doesn't have the knowledge that is stored in the context and needs to update itself to understand that knowledge as well. It's somehow a form of on-policy distillation happening inside the model.

As a summary, we have two phases. One is the generation, which generates some text about the knowledge in the context. The second part is on-policy distillation, where we distill the knowledge from one level to the other. That's what's happening in the training phase. We also have the self-modifying part, but I think that's the main idea of memory consolidation and how the training happened here.

items.question: How do you view the privacy and alignment implications of AI models that learn continually?

items.answer: Honestly, I don't have a very concrete idea about how it can be solved. From one side, the model is continually learning, so it can get all the information about you and use that, and it's really concerning. But on the other hand, if the model is designed properly, then it can use that information to align itself with your values, with everything that you want. I think generally these two directions of continual learning and privacy potentially are orthogonal, because all of the concerns in a static model can still happen in a continual learner. items.question: Why do you think having a variety of intelligent AI systems is preferable to having one system that learns about everything?
items.object: A diversity of intelligent AI systems
items.answer:
I personally think that there are huge challenges to make all these models very safe. I think there's a good point in the current AI environment, or at least in the research of AI environments. It seems to be very bad, but from another perspective it's also very good. There is no single way of defining what a model's intelligence is. Again, in my opinion, there is no way to say what is a continual learner. Every person can define their own way of what is continual learning, what model is called a continual learner, and so on. Similarly, we can say the same thing about intelligence. We might come up with different models, different architectures, different AI systems. Some people might say this one is intelligent, that one is not, and vice versa.

I think the good point is if we have different directions to explore, then we will come up with some AI systems, each with their own advantages and disadvantages. I think it can somehow provide a balance in the community and also in general society, because when something like that happens, we will understand that there is no single definition of intelligence. We are just one example of an intelligent system. There are other models, other ways that we can have more intelligent models and systems. One way to be smart is to be very adaptive. If you have a model that can adapt to its environment in a perfect way, it can simply be aligned to that context. That's great, but that's just one form of intelligence. Another is a model that has a lot of knowledge and know-how, and that model is fully aligned with human values, but potentially might not be able to solve mathematical problems. There's another model capable of mathematical reasoning, but it's not great if you want to search about daily stuff. You might come up with one benchmark and say that if some models achieve 100% accuracy, that specific model is intelligent, but another person can say other things. In general, I think when we have a variety of intelligent systems, including humans as one form of intelligence in this space—I'm not saying that's a perfect scenario—but it's better than having one single form of intelligence in the world and thinking about it to learn about everything and all these potential challenges.

items.question: Why do you find consciousness harder to discuss than reasoning?
items.object: Defining consciousness
items.answer:
I usually try to use terms that I can also define. For example, I might mistakenly use reasoning, but I have always wondered what is reasoning? I personally do not have a clear definition of what it means when we say something is doing reasoning. At least we have a clear common sense about the word reasoning. Even if we do not have a clear definition, when someone says this specific model is capable of doing reasoning, everyone more or less can understand what they are saying.

But the point about consciousness is that not only do we not have any clear definition of what consciousness is, but on the other hand, we don't even have a common sense about the word of consciousness. Everyone literally has their own way of defining consciousness. It's really hard to define what's conscious. I don't think that there might be a time when everyone could say something is definitely conscious or not, rather than humans, because for humans we have a common way to know that humans are conscious. I think it's really hard to argue that something is conscious or not.

items.question: How do you see active information processing connecting continual learning to consciousness?
items.object: Active information processing as a criterion for consciousness
items.answer: One thing that I personally have seen in all of the literature about what is considered a conscious being or not, I have seen one thing in common in every definition, as far as I know—I might be wrong—but I think the least level of criteria that we could say something is conscious is that the model or being is active. It has a form of active processing of information. In my opinion, that's the least criteria we can consider for a model or anything else to say it's a form of conscious model or something like that. items.answer: That's just my opinion, but I think we also discussed this in the conclusion of the paper: this learning is not a solution to continual learning.
